job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Here are the drafting problems I found in the October 6 text, numbered and keyed to section. I worked from the text alone, so please have legislative counsel confirm the statutory cross-references I mention at the end.

1. **§2(1)(A), volume threshold:** The 10,000-ton test applies "by a single vessel," so an operator can split output across several vessels that each stay under the line and fall outside the definition. Adding aggregation language for affiliated operators, fleets, and common ownership would close this.

2. **§2(1)(A), measurement:** The bill doesn't say whether 10,000 tons is measured wet or dry, as recovered nodules or total material handled, or at sea or at port. Nodules carry significant water, so the choice of basis could move reported volumes a lot.

3. **§2(1)(A), undefined terms:** "Polymetallic nodules," "other mineral resources," "seabed," and "recovery" are all undefined. This leaves open whether crust, sulphide, or sediment operations, and the handling of tailings and sediment, are covered.

4. **§2(1)(B), "Secretary" determinations:** The bill doesn't identify which Secretary decides, sets no criteria for "comparable" risk, and creates no notice, hearing, or review process. That invites both arbitrariness challenges and delay, and it gives the designated official broad discretion in either direction.

5. **§3(a), "engage in":** The prohibition doesn't say whether financing, chartering, equipment supply, insurance, or investment in covered activity counts. A company could argue that its role is supportive rather than operational.

6. **§2(2), "U.S. person":** Limiting the term to citizens and state-organized corporations leaves out LLCs, partnerships, and trusts, and it doesn't clearly reach foreign-organized holding companies or subsidiaries of U.S. groups. "State" is also undefined, so it's unclear whether D.C. and the territories are included.

7. **§2(3), "covered vessel":** The 5,000-gross-ton threshold has no relationship to the 10,000-ton production threshold, so a smaller vessel can mine at commercial scale without being registered or reporting. "Equipped for" is also undefined and doesn't clearly reach remotely operated collectors, support ships, or transfer vessels.

8. **§3(a), geographic scope:** "In the United States" doesn't say whether it includes the EEZ, the continental shelf, or the international Area. "Any U.S. person anywhere" doesn't reach foreign-flagged or foreign-controlled operations, which is the most likely structure for an offshore project.

9. **§3, no import or processing restriction:** The bill bans mining but not importing, processing, selling, or transporting nodules or metals recovered abroad. An operator could mine offshore under foreign sponsorship and ship product to U.S. refineries. A companion provision would close this.

10. **§3(b), pre-enactment exploration licenses:** The exemption covers any mining "conducted under an exploration license issued before" enactment, with no cap on tonnage, duration, renewal, amendment, or transfer, and no bar on commercial sales. A license issued shortly before enactment could support indefinite commercial mining. "Exploration license" and its issuing authority are also undefined.

11. **§3(b) with §8, the 180-day window:** Operations can expand or accelerate between enactment and the effective date, and nothing freezes new licenses, permits, or expansions during that period. The grandfathering in §3(b) makes that gap more valuable.

12. **§3(c), environmental assessment:** This exemption has no tonnage cap, no requirement for an approved plan or NOAA authorization, no reporting, and no bar on selling the material recovered. Commercial-scale extraction could be labeled "assessment," and this is likely the largest single gap in the bill.

13. **§4(a)–(b) and §5, no penalty for registry violations:** §5 penalizes only violations of §3, so failing to register a vessel or file a required report carries no penalty under the bill. The registry and reporting duties are therefore effectively voluntary.

14. **§4(b), report content:** Reports must be "certified by the operator," but the bill doesn't specify required data such as tonnage, location, depth, or sediment and plume monitoring. It also sets no accuracy standard, audit right, public availability requirement, or confidentiality rule, and "operator" is undefined.

15. **§4, monitoring gap:** Because reporting covers only covered vessels, mining by smaller vessels or non-vessel systems is invisible to NOAA. Together with items 1 and 7, this means violations may be hard to detect even where the prohibition applies.

16. **§5(a), penalty level and remedies:** The ceiling of $1,000,000 per day has no floor, no inflation adjustment, and no forfeiture of recovered material, vessels, or profits. The bill also gives no injunctive or cease-and-desist authority, so a company could treat the penalty as a cost of doing business.

17. **§5, enforcement machinery:** The bill names no enforcing agency or Attorney General role and sets no administrative penalty procedure. It also provides no inspection, boarding, or seizure authority, and no citizen suit provision, which makes enforcement beyond U.S. waters especially hard.

18. **§5(a), timing and accrual:** "For any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment" conflicts with §8, which delays §3 until 180 days after enactment, so it's unclear whether conduct in that window can be penalized. "Each day" is also undefined for continuing violations, and the bill doesn't say whether separate vessels or tonnage units count as separate violations.

19. **§5(b), criminal provisions:** "Willfully" is undefined, and the bill has no conspiracy, aiding-and-abetting, or responsible-corporate-officer language. Entity fines run through Title 18, which may be modest relative to the gains at stake (see the verification note below).

20. **§6, international agreement:** "Shall seek to negotiate" creates no consequence if negotiations fail and no obligation to report back. "Equivalent" is undefined, and the section doesn't address sponsored or foreign-flagged operations.

21. **§7(a), National Academies report:** Nothing requires the NAS to produce the report, sets a deadline, or funds the study. "Serious harm" has no metric, so if no report issues, it's unclear how the lifting standard could ever be satisfied.

22. **§7(a) vs. §7(b), internal conflict:** Subsection (a) keeps the prohibition in place until a joint resolution is enacted, but subsection (b) ends the entire Act after 10 years. The bill doesn't say which controls, and a court could read the sunset as ending the prohibition without any congressional finding.

23. **§7(b), no savings clause:** The sunset doesn't preserve enforcement for violations committed before it takes effect, and it says nothing about permits or operations that began during the Act. Without a savings clause, violations in the final years could go unpunished.

24. **§4 and §8, effective date of registry duties:** Section 4 sets no effective date or deadline for initial registration of existing vessels, so it presumably takes effect at the 180-day mark, but the bill doesn't say so.

25. **General provisions, missing:** The bill doesn't define "Secretary," "person," "operator," "United States," or "exploration license." It also has no severability clause, rulemaking authority, appropriations, judicial review provision, or statement of how it relates to the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act and existing NOAA permitting. Those conflicts could support a challenge on their own.

**Priorities for the markup:** Items 12 (environmental assessment exemption), 10 (pre-enactment licenses), 22–23 (sunset conflict and savings clause), 7–8 (vessel threshold and geographic scope), and 13–17 (enforcement gaps) are the most likely to matter in committee.

**Verification before anything goes to the Hill:** Have counsel check the 18 U.S.C. §3571 entity fine amounts, the 28 U.S.C. §2462 limitations period for civil penalties, the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. §1401 et seq.) interaction, and whether the joint resolution mechanism in §7(a) raises presentment or constitutional questions. I also haven't seen the prior version, so comparing the October 6 text against the redline would show which of these problems the manager's amendment introduced.
